Twin Peaks is a groundbreaking television drama that aired on ABC from 1990 to 1991 and later returned in limited form, establishing itself as one of the most influential and aesthetically daring series in television history. Created by filmmaker David Lynch and writer Mark Frost, the show blended murder mystery procedural with surrealism, horror, and absurdist humor, demonstrating that television could support complex, unconventional storytelling that challenged traditional narrative structures and audience expectations in fundamental ways.

The show premiered on ABC in April 1990 and ran for two seasons totaling thirty episodes, becoming a massive cultural phenomenon and an instant cultural touchstone despite its unconventional storytelling. It centered on the murder of homecoming queen Laura Palmer in the fictional small town of Twin Peaks, Washington. The investigation unfolds in ways that are both procedurally rigorous and increasingly surreal and supernatural. Kyle MacLachlan starred as FBI Special Agent Dale Cooper, whose fastidious manners, love of cherry pie and coffee, and spiritual intuition made him television's most distinctive and memorable detective.

The show's second season, responding to pressure to solve the central mystery, declined in quality when the network demanded resolution of Laura Palmer's murder. The show rebounded artistically with a David Lynch film continuation and later a 2017 limited series revival. Lynch directed much of the material personally and introduced a visual and tonal vocabulary combining noir detective conventions, horror, magical realism, and performance art aesthetics rarely seen on American network television before or since.

The show featured an ensemble cast of town eccentrics that turned the small town into a hall of quirky archetypes. There was a one-armed man with premonitions, the Log Lady obsessed with her Douglas fir log, and a gentle-hearted FBI receptionist among many others. These supporting characters became as iconic as the central mystery itself. The show influenced subsequent television series to attempt more ambitious, serialized, and unconventional narratives, demonstrating that audiences would follow complex, non-linear storytelling if it was compelling and stylistically distinctive.
